items.prompt: What does a SAST (Static Application Security Testing) tool actually examine?
choices: A running instance of the deployed application
The source code itself, without executing it
The list of third-party packages a project depends on
Network traffic between services in production
items.explanation: SAST reads source code text/structure directly, looking for known-dangerous shapes (string-built SQL, eval() on unsanitized input, hardcoded secrets) without ever running the program. That's what lets it run on every commit, before a build even happens.
items.reference:
SAST reads source code, never runs it — matches known-dangerous shapes like string-built SQL or eval()

Why: it can flag a bug the instant it's typed, before any build happens.

items.prompt: Team Aegis's pull request never merged because a scanner flagged a line building a SQL query with string concatenation. What kind of tool caught this, and when did it run?
choices: A DAST scanner, run against staging after deployment
A SAST scanner, run against the code in the pull request itself
A pentester, hired for a scheduled engagement
A fuzzer, run continuously against a parser
items.explanation: SAST scans source code as text/structure, so it runs directly against a pull request's diff before anything is built or deployed — exactly why Aegis's bug never reached staging at all.
items.reference:
SAST reads source code, never runs it — matches known-dangerous shapes like string-built SQL or eval()

Why: it can flag a bug the instant it's typed, before any build happens.

items.prompt: Which of these would a SAST tool most plausibly flag just by reading the code?
choices: A missing 'x-frame-options' response header on a live endpoint
A dependency version with a publicly known CVE
const query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " + userId;
A pentester social-engineering an employee over the phone
items.explanation: String-concatenated SQL is a textbook SAST pattern — a shape visible directly in the source text. The header issue needs a running server (DAST), the CVE needs a dependency scan (SCA), and social engineering needs a human (pentest).
items.reference:
SAST reads source code, never runs it — matches known-dangerous shapes like string-built SQL or eval()

Why: it can flag a bug the instant it's typed, before any build happens.

items.prompt: What does a DAST (Dynamic Application Security Testing) tool need in order to run at all?
choices: Read access to the application's source code repository
A running, deployed instance of the application to send requests to
A list of the application's third-party dependencies
A signed rules-of-engagement document
items.explanation: DAST doesn't read code — it sends real requests at something actually running (typically staging) and inspects the real responses, the way an outside attacker would. No deployed target means nothing to attack.
items.reference:
DAST attacks a running app from the outside — real requests, real responses, no access to source code

Why: it finds runtime issues (bad config, live injection) no static read of the code would show.

items.prompt: A tool sends malformed input to every field of a live staging endpoint and checks the responses for missing security headers and leaked stack traces. What type of tool is this?
choices: SCA
SAST
DAST
Fuzzing, specifically
items.explanation: Attacking a running instance from the outside via real HTTP requests, and inspecting real responses, is exactly what DAST does — it has no visibility into source code at all, only what the running app exposes over the wire.
items.reference:
DAST attacks a running app from the outside — real requests, real responses, no access to source code

Why: it finds runtime issues (bad config, live injection) no static read of the code would show.

items.prompt: Why can't DAST run at commit time, the way SAST does?
choices: DAST is slower to configure than SAST, nothing more
DAST needs something actually deployed and running to send requests at — nothing exists yet at commit time
DAST only works on databases, not web applications
DAST requires a human tester to operate it manually
items.explanation: DAST's entire method is sending real requests at a live target and reading real responses. At commit time there is no running instance yet — that's precisely why DAST sits later in the pipeline, typically against staging.
items.reference:
DAST attacks a running app from the outside — real requests, real responses, no access to source code

Why: it finds runtime issues (bad config, live injection) no static read of the code would show.

items.prompt: Aegis had clean SAST and DAST scans for six months, then a pentest found that setting order quantity to a negative number caused the checkout flow to pay the customer instead of charge them. Why didn't any automated scanner catch this?
choices: The scanners were misconfigured and needed a higher severity threshold
Automated scanners match known code/traffic patterns; nothing about a negative quantity looks like a known-dangerous pattern, it's a judgment call about what the business logic should allow
The bug was introduced after the last scan ran
DAST tools cannot test checkout flows at all
items.explanation: Pattern-matching tools recognize shapes: string-built SQL, missing headers, known-CVE dependency versions. 'A quantity shouldn't be allowed to go negative here' isn't a pattern at all — it's a rule about what the system was supposed to permit, which only a human reasoning about intent can evaluate.
items.reference:
Aegis: clean SAST, clean DAST, still breached — a negative order quantity paid the customer at checkout

Why: no scanner has a pattern for 'this number shouldn't be allowed to be negative here.'

items.prompt: What is the practical implication of 'automated scanners can't catch business-logic flaws'?
choices: Automated scanning is not worth doing since it misses so much
A clean SAST/DAST/SCA result means the system is fully secure
A clean automated scan result means no *known-pattern* bug was found — it says nothing about logic flaws, which still need a human evaluating intent
Business-logic flaws are rare enough to ignore in most systems
items.explanation: The scanners are still valuable — they catch the cheap, common bugs constantly and for almost no cost. But 'clean scan' only means 'no known pattern matched,' not 'secure' — which is exactly why a periodic pentest with a human reasoning about the product's actual rules still finds things scanners structurally cannot.
items.reference:
Aegis: clean SAST, clean DAST, still breached — a negative order quantity paid the customer at checkout

Why: no scanner has a pattern for 'this number shouldn't be allowed to be negative here.'

items.prompt: Which of these is most likely to be found by a human pentester rather than any automated scanner?
choices: A dependency version with a known, published CVE
A missing 'strict-transport-security' response header
Chaining a discount code with a return policy to receive a product for free and a refund at the same time
A hardcoded API key left in a config file
items.explanation: Chaining two individually-legitimate features (a discount and a return) into a net-negative outcome for the business is a judgment call about intent and process — no automated tool has a pattern for 'these two allowed actions combine into an unintended outcome.' The other three are all textbook automated-tool findings (SCA, DAST, and SAST respectively).
items.reference:
Aegis: clean SAST, clean DAST, still breached — a negative order quantity paid the customer at checkout

Why: no scanner has a pattern for 'this number shouldn't be allowed to be negative here.'

items.prompt: A SAST rule flags `const q = "SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = " + orderId;` even though `orderId` is always an internally-generated integer that can never contain attacker input. What is this an example of?
choices: A false negative
A false positive
A true negative
A critical severity finding that should be ignored
items.explanation: The tool flagged something that, in this specific case, isn't actually exploitable — that's a false positive. The pattern (string concatenation into SQL) is usually dangerous, so the rule still fires; it just can't see that this particular input source is safe.
items.reference:
False positive

flagged, but not actually a problem

False negative

real problem, tool stayed silent

Why: loosening a rule to kill false positives usually creates false negatives.

items.prompt: A SAST scanner has no rule for detecting SQL built inside a helper function two calls away from the query itself, so it stays silent on a real injection vulnerability hidden that way. What is this an example of?
choices: A false positive
A true positive
A false negative
An expected and harmless gap
items.explanation: A real vulnerability existed and the tool reported nothing — that's a false negative. Simple pattern matchers are especially prone to this once the dangerous pattern is hidden behind a function boundary the tool doesn't trace through.
items.reference:
False positive

flagged, but not actually a problem

False negative

real problem, tool stayed silent

Why: loosening a rule to kill false positives usually creates false negatives.

items.prompt: How does a bug bounty program differ from a scheduled pentest engagement?
choices: A bug bounty is always cheaper than a pentest
A bug bounty runs continuously and opportunistically, rewarding any outside researcher who finds a real bug; a pentest is a scoped, time-boxed engagement scheduled periodically
A bug bounty only accepts findings from automated scanners
A pentest can only be run once per company, ever
items.explanation: A pentest is scoped and scheduled — a specific team, a specific window, guaranteed coverage of what was agreed. A bug bounty is standing and open-ended — no guaranteed coverage of any particular area, but always-on incentive for someone to look, indefinitely.
items.reference:
Pentest

scoped, time-boxed, scheduled a few times a year

Bug bounty

open, ongoing, continuous

Why: a bounty adds always-on coverage a periodic engagement can't.

items.prompt: What is a real limitation of a bug bounty program compared to a scheduled pentest?
choices: Bug bounties never find real vulnerabilities
A bug bounty has no obligation to cover any specific part of the system — coverage is opportunistic, not guaranteed, unlike a scoped pentest
Bug bounty researchers are never paid for valid findings
Bug bounties can only run for a fixed number of days
items.explanation: Nobody is assigned to test any particular feature in a bounty program — researchers look wherever they choose. That's why it complements, rather than replaces, a scheduled pentest: the pentest guarantees a specific scope gets deliberate attention.
items.reference:
Pentest

scoped, time-boxed, scheduled a few times a year

Bug bounty

open, ongoing, continuous

Why: a bounty adds always-on coverage a periodic engagement can't.

items.prompt: In the shift-left pipeline, which pair is correctly ordered from earliest to latest?
choices: DAST at commit, SAST at staging
SAST at commit, DAST at staging
Pentest at commit, SAST at staging
SCA at staging, SAST at build
items.explanation: SAST reads source code, so it can run the instant code is written — at commit/PR time. DAST needs something running, so it can only fire once a build has reached staging. That ordering is exactly why 'shift left' means moving cheap checks earlier, not the reverse.
items.reference:
Commit→SAST, Build→SCA, Staging→DAST, Periodic→Pentest, Continuous→Bug bounty

Why: earlier = cheaper fix, later = deeper but slower/costlier check.

items.prompt: Why does SCA typically run at build time rather than at commit time, alongside SAST?
choices: SCA needs the exact resolved set of dependency versions that only exists once a build/install step has happened
SCA is slower than SAST for no particular reason
SCA requires a deployed, running instance like DAST does
SCA can only run once a year
items.explanation: SCA checks the exact dependency versions about to be built against known-vulnerability databases — that resolved version list is only fully known once an install/build step runs, so it sits just after SAST rather than at the same instant.
items.reference:
Commit→SAST, Build→SCA, Staging→DAST, Periodic→Pentest, Continuous→Bug bounty

Why: earlier = cheaper fix, later = deeper but slower/costlier check.

items.prompt: Where does manual pentesting sit in the shift-left pipeline, and why not earlier?
choices: At commit time, because it's the cheapest check available
Periodically, later than DAST — it requires a human's scheduled time and judgment, which is slow and expensive compared to any automated check
Continuously, running on every single commit
It doesn't fit anywhere in the pipeline, it's unrelated to shift-left
items.explanation: A pentest needs a person reasoning about intent, not a pattern match — that's slow and expensive per run, so it happens periodically (quarterly/yearly) rather than on every commit the way SAST does. The trade-off is depth (it catches what automation can't) for frequency.
items.reference:
Commit→SAST, Build→SCA, Staging→DAST, Periodic→Pentest, Continuous→Bug bounty

Why: earlier = cheaper fix, later = deeper but slower/costlier check.

items.prompt: What exactly does SCA scan, and what is it checking each item against?
choices: Your own application source code, against known-dangerous patterns
Your third-party dependencies' versions, against public vulnerability databases
Your running staging environment, against known attack payloads
Your CI configuration, against a list of best practices
items.explanation: SCA never reads the code you wrote — it inventories the exact versions of every dependency you're about to build and checks each against public vulnerability databases (like the NVD) for known, published flaws.
items.reference:
SCA checks dependency versions against known-CVE databases — it doesn't read your own code at all

Why: a brand-new, unpublished flaw in a dependency won't have a CVE yet, so SCA won't catch it either.

items.prompt: A dependency your app uses has a serious flaw that was discovered by an attacker and exploited in the wild, but no CVE has been published for it yet. Will a routine SCA scan flag this dependency?
choices: Yes, SCA scans the actual code of every dependency for dangerous patterns
No — SCA checks versions against databases of *already-published* known vulnerabilities; an unpublished flaw has nothing to match against yet
Yes, but only if the dependency is a direct dependency, not transitive
No, SCA only scans dependencies written in the same language as your app
items.explanation: SCA's entire method is version-to-database matching. A flaw with no published CVE yet is invisible to it by construction — the same structural gap that let a supply-chain compromise with no CVE slip through untouched (see the sibling unit `supply-chain-security` for the deeper trust-chain problem behind this).
items.reference:
SCA checks dependency versions against known-CVE databases — it doesn't read your own code at all

Why: a brand-new, unpublished flaw in a dependency won't have a CVE yet, so SCA won't catch it either.

items.prompt: Which finding is a realistic DAST result?
choices: A version of a logging library with a known CVE
A missing 'strict-transport-security' response header on a live staging endpoint
A business rule that lets two legitimate discounts combine into a net loss
A hardcoded password visible only in source code, never in any response
items.explanation: DAST inspects real responses from a running app — a missing security header is exactly the kind of thing visible in an HTTP response. The CVE example is SCA's job, the combined-discount rule needs human judgment (pentest), and a secret that never appears in any response is invisible to a tool that only sees traffic.
items.reference:
DAST catches runtime issues (headers, live injection, error leaks) but only what it thought to try, against something already deployed

Why: a clean DAST scan means no known attack pattern worked, not 'this app is safe.'

items.prompt: Aegis ran DAST against staging for six months with zero findings. Does that mean the running application has no exploitable request path at all?
choices: Yes, a clean DAST scan is proof the application is fully secure
No — it means no request shape or pattern the tool knows to try succeeded; DAST has no way to reason about business rules or intent
Yes, but only for the specific endpoints tested, everything else is unknown (this is the only correct caveat)
No, because DAST never actually sends real requests, only simulates them
items.explanation: DAST tries known attack patterns against real endpoints. 'Clean' means those specific known patterns didn't work — it says nothing about a business-logic flaw like Aegis's negative-quantity refund, which isn't a request *shape* problem at all, just an allowed value nobody should have allowed.
items.reference:
DAST catches runtime issues (headers, live injection, error leaks) but only what it thought to try, against something already deployed

Why: a clean DAST scan means no known attack pattern worked, not 'this app is safe.'

items.prompt: Why can't DAST catch a vulnerability hidden behind a code path that's never actually exercised by any request during the scan window?
choices: DAST reads the source code directly, so this shouldn't matter
DAST only observes behavior through requests and responses — a code path it never triggers produces no observable behavior to flag
DAST intentionally skips rarely-used code paths to save time
This isn't actually a limitation of DAST
items.explanation: DAST has no visibility into code at all — only into what a running app actually does in response to the requests it sends. A path never triggered during the scan simply never produces any signal for the tool to act on.
items.reference:
DAST catches runtime issues (headers, live injection, error leaks) but only what it thought to try, against something already deployed

Why: a clean DAST scan means no known attack pattern worked, not 'this app is safe.'

items.prompt: Why does pentesting happen a few times a year instead of on every commit, the way SAST does?
choices: Pentesting is technically incapable of running more often than that
Pentesting trades frequency for depth: it needs a human's expensive time to find what automation can't, so it can't be as cheap or frequent as a pattern match
Companies are legally required to limit pentests to a fixed schedule
Pentesting only works on systems that change slowly
items.explanation: The cost/speed/depth trade-off is one dial, not three separate facts: the deeper a technique's reasoning (a human considering intent vs. a regex matching a shape), the slower and more expensive each run is, which is exactly why it runs less often.
items.reference:
⚡ Fast + cheap + shallow — SAST, SCA
⏳ Slower + costlier + deeper — DAST, fuzzing
👤 Slowest + costliest + deepest — Pentest

Why: depth and frequency trade off directly, not independently.

items.prompt: A team wants to run a full pentest-style human review on every single pull request, matching SAST's frequency. What's the direct trade-off they'd be making?
choices: None — more frequent human review is strictly better with no downside
They'd be paying a slow, expensive resource at a frequency it was never built for — the entire reason automated checks exist first is to keep the cheap, common bugs off a human's plate
Pentesting can only be scheduled once per calendar year by definition
Pull requests are not a valid target for pentesting
items.explanation: Depth and frequency are opposite ends of the same trade-off. Running the deepest, most expensive technique at the highest frequency defeats the point of layering — automated checks exist specifically to filter out the cheap bugs so scarce human attention goes toward what only humans can find.
items.reference:
⚡ Fast + cheap + shallow — SAST, SCA
⏳ Slower + costlier + deeper — DAST, fuzzing
👤 Slowest + costliest + deepest — Pentest

Why: depth and frequency trade off directly, not independently.

items.prompt: What is the most accurate way to interpret a fully clean SAST + DAST + SCA result across the board?
choices: The system is definitively secure against any attack
No pattern any of these three tools knows to check for was found — business-logic and novel flaws remain untested by construction
Only DAST results matter; SAST and SCA are redundant once DAST is clean
The system no longer needs a pentest, since three tools already passed
items.explanation: Each of the three tools checks a specific, known category of pattern. A clean result across all three narrows the field of *known* pattern-based bugs to zero — it says nothing about business-logic flaws or anything outside what those tools were built to recognize.
items.reference:
Clean SAST + clean DAST for 6 months — still breached via a business-logic flaw a pentest found

Why: 'no known pattern matched' isn't the same claim as 'secure.'

items.prompt: Aegis's negative-quantity refund bug existed the entire six months their scans were clean. What does this timeline actually demonstrate?
choices: The scanners were buggy and needed to be replaced
A vulnerability can exist and be exploitable for a long time even while every automated check passes, because the check was never built to look for that category of flaw
Six months is an unusually long gap between pentests, which caused the problem
DAST scans expire after a fixed time and Aegis's had lapsed
items.explanation: Nothing about the scanners malfunctioned — they correctly reported zero *known-pattern* findings, the whole time, because a business-logic flaw was never a pattern they check for in the first place. The gap wasn't a tooling failure; it's the structural limit L2's comparison table names directly.
items.reference:
Clean SAST + clean DAST for 6 months — still breached via a business-logic flaw a pentest found

Why: 'no known pattern matched' isn't the same claim as 'secure.'

items.prompt: If a team wanted to close the exact gap that let Aegis's refund bug go undetected for six months, which addition to their existing SAST+DAST+SCA setup would actually address it?
choices: Running SAST twice as often
Adding a periodic pentest, where a human deliberately reasons about what the business logic should and shouldn't allow
Lowering DAST's severity threshold so more findings get reported
Switching to a different SAST vendor with more rules
items.explanation: More frequent or more sensitive pattern-matching still only matches patterns — it can't reason about intent. Only a human evaluating what the checkout flow was actually supposed to allow (a pentest) can catch a flaw defined entirely by 'this shouldn't have been allowed,' not by any recognizable shape.
items.reference:
Clean SAST + clean DAST for 6 months — still breached via a business-logic flaw a pentest found

Why: 'no known pattern matched' isn't the same claim as 'secure.'

items.prompt: Implement `detectEvalUsage(line)`. Return `true` if the line calls `eval(` anywhere (with any amount of whitespace before the parenthesis), `false` otherwise. This is the exact rule from the L3 scanner's `RULES` array.

tests.description: detects direct eval call
detects eval with whitespace before parens
ignores unrelated code
ignores a comment mentioning eval as a word only
tests.expr: expect(detectEvalUsage('// never use eval for this')).toBe(false)

items.explanation: The `\b` word boundary stops 'evaluate(' from matching (no boundary right before '('), while `\s*` allows any amount of whitespace between 'eval' and the opening parenthesis, matching both `eval(x)` and `eval (x)`. A plain comment mentioning the word 'eval' with no parenthesis at all never matches, since the pattern requires the literal call syntax.
items.reference:
A SAST rule is just: does this line match a known-dangerous shape? eval(...), string-built SQL, a hardcoded secret

Why: the pattern is checked per line, with no understanding of where the value actually came from.

items.prompt: Implement `detectHardcodedSecret(line)`. Return `true` if the line assigns a quoted string of 8+ alphanumeric/underscore/hyphen characters to a variable named (case-insensitively) `api_key`, `apikey`, `secret`, or `password`, `false` otherwise.

tests.description: detects a hardcoded api key
detects password assignment
ignores a value loaded from env
ignores a short/non-secret-looking string

items.explanation: The pattern requires the variable name shape, an `=`, and a quoted literal of at least 8 characters — `process.env.API_KEY` never matches because there's no quoted string literal on the right-hand side at all, only an expression. This is the same trade-off as every SAST rule: it recognizes the shape of a hardcoded value, not whether the value is genuinely a secret.
items.reference:
A SAST rule is just: does this line match a known-dangerous shape? eval(...), string-built SQL, a hardcoded secret

Why: the pattern is checked per line, with no understanding of where the value actually came from.

items.prompt: Implement `detectSqlConcat(line)`. Return `true` if the line looks like a SQL keyword (SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) inside a quoted string that is being concatenated with `+`, in either direction (`"SELECT..." + x` or `x + "SELECT..."`), `false` otherwise.

tests.description: detects string-first concatenation
tests.expr: expect(detectSqlConcat("const q = 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ' + orderId;")).toBe(true)

tests.description: detects concatenation into an INSERT
tests.expr: expect(detectSqlConcat('const q = "INSERT INTO logs VALUES (" + val + ")";')).toBe(true)

tests.description: ignores a parameterized query
tests.expr: expect(detectSqlConcat("const q = 'SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = ?';")).toBe(false)

tests.description: ignores unrelated string concatenation

items.explanation: This is the exact rule that blocked Aegis's pull request: a quoted string containing a SQL keyword, adjacent to a `+`, in either order. It's a shape match only — it has no idea whether `orderId` is attacker-controlled or an internally-generated integer, which is why this exact rule can also produce false positives on safe concatenations of the same shape.
items.reference:
A SAST rule is just: does this line match a known-dangerous shape? eval(...), string-built SQL, a hardcoded secret

Why: the pattern is checked per line, with no understanding of where the value actually came from.

items.prompt: Implement `countCrashes(fn, inputs)`. Call `fn` once for each value in the `inputs` array, catching any thrown error. Return the total number of inputs that caused `fn` to throw.

tests.description: counts zero when nothing crashes
counts every crashing input
tests.expr: expect(countCrashes((x) => { if (x < 0) throw new Error('neg'); return x; }, [1,-1,2,-2])).toBe(2)

tests.description: counts all as crashing if fn always throws

items.explanation: This is the counting core of a fuzz harness: run the target on every input inside a try/catch, and tally what throws. Real fuzzers add randomized/mutated input generation on top of this exact loop — the crash-detection mechanism itself is this simple.
items.reference:
Fuzzing = run the target function on many inputs, catch what makes it throw — no pattern knowledge needed

Why: volume finds edge cases no one thought to write a test for.

items.prompt: Implement `firstCrashingInput(fn, inputs)`. Return the first value in `inputs` that causes `fn` to throw when called with it, or `null` if none of them crash.

tests.description: returns null when nothing crashes
returns the first crashing input, not a later one
tests.expr: expect(firstCrashingInput((x) => { if (x < 0) throw new Error('neg'); return x; }, [1,2,-3,-4])).toBe(-3)

tests.description: returns the only input if it crashes

items.explanation: Returning on the first thrown error, rather than continuing the loop, is exactly what a fuzz harness does when it wants a minimal reproducible failing case to hand back to a developer — the earliest crash found is usually reported first and investigated before continuing the run.
items.reference:
Fuzzing = run the target function on many inputs, catch what makes it throw — no pattern knowledge needed

Why: volume finds edge cases no one thought to write a test for.

items.prompt: Implement `crashRate(fn, inputs)`. Return the percentage (0-100, rounded to the nearest whole number) of inputs that cause `fn` to throw when called with them. Return `0` if `inputs` is empty.

tests.description: returns 0 for an empty input list
returns 0 when nothing crashes
returns 50 when half the inputs crash
tests.expr: expect(crashRate((x) => { if (x < 0) throw new Error('neg'); return x; }, [1,-1,2,-2])).toBe(50)

tests.description: returns 100 when everything crashes

items.explanation: This is the same crash-detection loop as the other two variants in this pool, just reduced to a single summary percentage instead of a count or the first offending input — a real fuzz harness typically reports all three views of the same underlying run.
items.reference:
Fuzzing = run the target function on many inputs, catch what makes it throw — no pattern knowledge needed

Why: volume finds edge cases no one thought to write a test for.

items.prompt: Implement `findMissingHeaders(headers, required)`. `headers` is an object of response header names (lowercase keys) to values. `required` is an array of lowercase header names that must be present. Return an array of the required header names that are missing from `headers`, in the same order as `required`.

tests.description: returns empty array when all required headers present
returns the missing header names
returns all required headers if none present

items.explanation: This is the exact check the L3 prober runs per endpoint: for each required security header, is it present in the response at all. The prober has no idea *why* a header is missing (misconfiguration vs. an intentional exception) — it only reports the observable gap.
items.reference:
A DAST-style header check just diffs a required-headers list against what the response actually sent back

Why: it only reasons about what's observable over the wire, never source code.

items.prompt: Implement `hasSecurityHeader(headers, name)`. `headers` is an object of lowercase header names to values. Return `true` if `name` (also lowercase) is present in `headers` AND its value is a non-empty string, `false` otherwise.

tests.description: true when header present with a value
false when header missing entirely
false when header present but empty string

items.explanation: A header technically present but set to an empty string is functionally the same as missing — a real server misconfiguration can produce exactly this, so a check that only tests `name in headers` would silently pass a broken response. Checking for a genuinely non-empty value is what a real DAST tool actually verifies.
items.reference:
A DAST-style header check just diffs a required-headers list against what the response actually sent back

Why: it only reasons about what's observable over the wire, never source code.

items.prompt: Implement `countMissingHeaders(headers, required)`. Same inputs as the other variants in this pool — return the *number* (not the list) of required headers missing from `headers`.

tests.description: returns 0 when all present
returns correct count when some missing
returns full length when required list is empty against any headers

items.explanation: Same filter as the list-returning variant in this pool, reduced to a count — useful when a CI gate just needs a number to compare against a threshold (e.g. 'fail if more than 0 required headers are missing') rather than the specific names.
items.reference:
A DAST-style header check just diffs a required-headers list against what the response actually sent back

Why: it only reasons about what's observable over the wire, never source code.

items.prompt: Implement `shouldBlockMerge(findings, threshold)`. `findings` is an array of `{ severity }` objects, each severity one of `'low'`, `'medium'`, `'high'`, `'critical'` (in increasing order). Return `true` if any finding's severity is at or above `threshold`, `false` otherwise.

tests.description: blocks when a finding meets the threshold exactly
blocks when a finding exceeds the threshold
does not block when all findings are below threshold
does not block with no findings at all

items.explanation: This is `--fail-on=high` from the CI YAML made literal: compare each finding's position in the ordered severity list against the threshold's position, and block if any finding is at or past it. The threshold is a deliberate policy choice — too low and every PR is blocked by noise, too high and real bugs merge silently.
items.reference:
Severity order: low < medium < high < critical — a gate blocks the merge if any finding is at or above the threshold

Why: gating on everything drowns the team in noise; gating on nothing makes the scanner decoration.

items.prompt: Implement `highestSeverity(findings)`. `findings` is an array of `{ severity }` objects using the order `'low' < 'medium' < 'high' < 'critical'`. Return the single highest severity string present, or `null` if `findings` is empty.

tests.description: returns null for empty findings
returns the single severity present

items.explanation: A CI gate summary often wants to report the single worst finding to a developer rather than the full list — reducing over the same ordered severity list used for the threshold check finds that maximum directly.
items.reference:
Severity order: low < medium < high < critical — a gate blocks the merge if any finding is at or above the threshold

Why: gating on everything drowns the team in noise; gating on nothing makes the scanner decoration.

items.prompt: Implement `filterBySeverity(findings, minSeverity)`. `findings` is an array of `{ severity }` objects using the order `'low' < 'medium' < 'high' < 'critical'`. Return only the findings whose severity is at or above `minSeverity`, preserving their original order.

tests.description: filters out findings below the minimum
keeps findings equal to the minimum
preserves original order among kept findings

items.explanation: This is the same comparison as `shouldBlockMerge`, but returning the qualifying findings themselves rather than a single boolean — useful for a report that shows a developer exactly which findings triggered the gate, not just that it was triggered.

items.prompt: Implement `slaForSeverity(severity)` using the remediation SLA table from L3: `critical` → 7 days, `high` → 30, `medium` → 90, `low` → 180. Return the number of days, or `null` for any severity not in the table.

tests.description: critical is 7 days
high is 30 days
medium is 90 days
unknown severity returns null

items.explanation: This is the L3 remediation table as a lookup: the same severity that decided Aegis's refund bug got a 7-day fix window (critical) also decides every other finding's urgency, regardless of whether an automated scan or a human pentester found it.
items.reference:
critical: 7 days · high: 30 · medium: 90 · low: 180 — a real pentest remediation SLA table

Why: severity determines urgency, not which stage found the bug.

items.prompt: Implement `isOverdue(severity, daysSinceReported)`, using the same SLA table (`critical`: 7, `high`: 30, `medium`: 90, `low`: 180 days). Return `true` if `daysSinceReported` has exceeded that severity's SLA, `false` if it hasn't (or if `severity` isn't in the table).

tests.description: not overdue when within the SLA window
overdue once past the SLA window
exactly at the SLA boundary is not yet overdue
unknown severity is never reported as overdue

items.explanation: This is what actually drives a remediation-tracking dashboard: a finding becomes overdue the moment it's been open longer than its severity's SLA allows, with the boundary day itself (`daysSinceReported === SLA`) still counted as on-time, not yet overdue.
